extracted.intended_audience: ICML 2026 reviewers and authors (conference peer-review participants)
extracted.subtask_description: Policy document defining permitted and prohibited uses of LLMs in ICML 2026 peer review via a two-policy (Policy A conservative / Policy B permissive) framework, plus implementation, declaration, and enforcement guidance for matching reviewers and submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy A (Conservative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of LLMs for reviewing is strictly prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can require their papers be reviewed under Policy A; any reviewer who is an author on a paper that requires Policy A must also be willing to follow Policy A. Submissions are matched with compatible reviewers. Enforcement faces similar challenges as previous conference LLM bans, but the conference expects less adversarial compliance since reviewers can opt in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy B (Permissive) — allowed and not allowed uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowed: Use of LLMs to help understand the paper and related works, and polish reviews. Submissions can be fed to privacy-compliant LLMs. Not allowed: Ask LLMs about strengths/weaknesses, ask to suggest key points for the review, suggest an outline for the review, write the full review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The assessment of the paper and the writing of the review must not be delegated to LLMs. Summarization (as a way to delegate judgment) is disallowed. Allowing polishing complicates detection/enforcement because some LLM-detection tools cannot be used if polishing is permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer responsibility for review content
rubrics_metrics.description: Under both policies, reviewers are always responsible for the full content of their reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an LLM is used for allowed activities (e.g., polishing), the reviewer remains fully accountable for correctness, judgments, and any content (including factual claims). Instances of hallucinated content constitute a clear violation of the LLM policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration and matching process
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers declare which policy they want to follow, and authors declare whether they require their papers to be reviewed under Policy A or allow them to be reviewed under Policy B. Submissions are matched with compatible reviewers; each reviewer is told which policy to follow on all of their assigned papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This matching enforces compatibility (e.g., reviewers who prefer/are willing to follow A will be assigned papers that require A). The conference extends its reciprocal reviewing requirement to support sufficient reviewers for Policy A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'privacy-compliant' LLMs
rubrics_metrics.description: By “privacy-compliant”, we refer to LLM tools that do not use logged data for training and that place limits on data retention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes enterprise/institutional subscriptions to LLM APIs, consumer subscriptions with an explicit opt-out from training, and self-hosted LLMs. The policy notes this is an oversimplification and that some aspects (e.g., true compliance) may be hard to verify/enforce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowed activities under Policy B (specific permitted uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitted activities include: polishing reviewer-written text, concept/background clarification, and related-work search; reviewers may input submission text into privacy-compliant LLMs for these purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey evidence: ~70% of respondents likely to use LLMs for polishing; concept/background clarification and related-work search were also top activities. The policy explicitly allows these to support reviewers where they are, while retaining human assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disallowed activities under Policy B (specific prohibited uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disallowed uses include: asking LLMs about strengths/weaknesses of the submission, asking LLMs to suggest key points for the review, asking LLMs to suggest an outline for the review, writing the full review, and using LLMs for summarization that substitutes for human assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These activities are disallowed because they delegate substantive judgment or composition of critiques to LLMs, which conflicts with the goal of retaining human assessment as crucial to the reviewing process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal reviewing augmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The existing reciprocal reviewing policy (each submission must nominate one of its authors as a reviewer) is augmented so that any reviewer who is an author on a paper that requires Policy A must be willing to follow Policy A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This design choice aims to ensure a sufficient pool of reviewers willing to follow Policy A and is framed as a fair extension of reciprocity to encourage buy-in and compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforceability, detection, and penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: The policy acknowledges enforcement limitations: some parts (e.g., verifying privacy-compliance of an LLM) are not realistically enforceable. The conference will use automated tools to help detect LLM use while respecting confidentiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flagging by tools is not immediate proof of violation (false positives; many LLM uses allowed under Policy B). However, hallucinated content is a clear violation; low-quality reviews may violate the reciprocal reviewing policy and be treated as abuse. Reported violations will be penalized, and the conference relies to a degree on reviewers' honesty (similar to confidentiality obligations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design goals and guiding principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The policy is guided by these goals: retain human assessment as crucial; meet reviewers where they are in their use of AI; respect authors who do not want their papers fed to LLMs; uphold integrity and transparency of the peer-review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These principles motivated the dual-policy framework (to balance differing community preferences) and the decision to allow limited LLM uses (e.g., polishing) while prohibiting delegation of assessment and critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk management and expected non-compliance considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys indicate non-negligible but not rampant non-compliance risk; some reviewers would be hampered by a strict ban and might opt out of reviewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy design accounts for these trade-offs: offering Policy B reduces reviewer attrition risk; Policy A is available for authors who require it; the conference expects to monitor compliance but acknowledges imperfect enforcement and the need to trust reviewers to an extent.
